newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Zairean leaders to hold talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Zairean leaders to hold talks.

text.p: The United States said it was not confident a meeting between Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila would take place as planned on Friday and urged the two men to hold the talks.

"These talks are very important for President Mobutu, very important for alliance leader Kabila. But most importantly, very important for the people of Zaire. We believe it is essential that these talks take place. And we urge the leaders to make that happen," John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, told reporters.

Witnesses reported that Mobutu boarded a South African navy ship in Congo on Friday for talks with his civil war rival Kabila. However, an official source in Angola said Kabila had pulled out of the summit and was returning to his base in the Zairean city of Lubumbashi.

The source in Angola said South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki "has gone back to the boat to explain that Kabila is not coming tonight. Kabila is not happy with the arrangements. I can't go into what that is."

"My understanding is that Kabila is leaving or has left already for (Zairean rebel headquarters city of) Lubumbashi. We'll try to reconstruct this whole thing later, but obviously it's going to be very difficult," he said.

Dinger, speaking before the report from Angola on Kabila's decision, said: "I think since the meeting has not yet begun and since at least Mr. Kabila's travel would involve a relatively lengthy helicopter flight to his ship, I think we have to be frank and realise that it is very much in question whether the meeting is going to take place today."

Dinger refused to discuss reports that France had mounted a covert operation to try to keep Mobutu, whose hold on power has been eroding under a rebel advance, in power. Instead, he stressed the United States and France "have worked very, very closely throughout this crisis...(and) share the same objectives in Zaire."

Those objectives are obtaining a cessation of hostilities; seeing a negotiated transition to a democratic government; responding to the urgent humanitarian needs of refugees in Eastern Zaire; and facilitating the repatriation of Rwandan refugees, the spokesman said.

Mobutu, one of Africa's last veteran strongmen but whose grip on Zaire is crumbling after three decades in power, went onto the Russian-built ice-breaker five hours late after poor health prevented him climbing 31 steep metal steps to board.

He was driven up a make-shift ramp onto the SAS Outeniqua, where South Africa's President Nelson Mandela was waiting to host the talks. The ship then left port, sailing toward international waters off the Angola-Zaire border to pick up Kabila.
Bill Richardson, Washington's ambassador to the United Nations who was sent to Zaire as special U.S. troubleshooter, was with Mandela, who asked him to participate in the talks.

Dinger reiterated the U.S. belief that Angola "has been providing support to the (rebel) alliance" but he refused to confirm a Washington Post report that Angolan troops equipped with armoured vehicles and heavy artillery have joined Zairean rebels in their push toward the capital Kinshasa.

He said, however, that the United States has been deeply concerned about the possibility of the Zairean civil war spreading across borders and have repeatedly asked Angola and other neighbouring countries to stay out of the fight.

This is a major reason why Richardson visited Luanda this week to "underscore in the strongest terms that we believe it is clearly in Angola's interest not to become involved in Zaire, because that involvement is only likely to contribute to unrest in Zaire, which borders on Angola," he said.
If the war were to spread across Zaire's boundaries "it's very difficult to say what the impact could be," Dinger said.
"We believe this is a conflict that must be resolved -- must be limited to the people of Zaire, and must be resolved by them," he added.
